final_note: You worked through Physics — Energy changes in systems — 11 specification statements.

concepts.def: The object, or group of objects, whose energy is being considered. In this section the system is the material whose temperature changes — for example a metal block, or the water in a beaker.
The energy stored in, or released from, a system as its temperature changes, measured in joules, J. It is a change, not a total: it does not say how much energy the system stores altogether.

concepts.term: Word equation for a temperature change
concepts.def: change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity × temperature change. All three factors multiply, so leaving one out, or dividing by one of them, makes the answer wrong by that whole factor.
The symbol form of the same equation: ∆E is the change in thermal energy, m the mass, c the specific heat capacity and ∆θ the temperature change. The symbol ∆ always means 'change in'.
The mass of the material whose temperature changes, in kilograms, kg. A mass given in grams must be divided by 1000 before it is used, because the unit of c already contains 'per kilogram'.

The amount of energy required to raise the temperature of one kilogram of a substance by one degree Celsius. It is a property of the substance, so every sample of that substance has the same value whatever its mass.

The unit of specific heat capacity: joules per kilogram per degree Celsius. The unit is a direct reading of the definition — joules of energy, for each kilogram, for each degree Celsius of temperature rise.
The difference between the final and the starting temperature, in degrees Celsius, °C. It is found by subtraction before the equation is used, and it is never the final temperature on its own.

An investigation to determine the specific heat capacity of one or more materials by linking the decrease of one energy store (or work done) to the rise in temperature and so to the increase in thermal energy stored. Measuring the energy supplied, the mass and the temperature rise gives c = ∆E ÷ (m × ∆θ).

Energy that leaves the heated block or liquid and warms the room instead. It makes the measured temperature rise smaller than the supplied energy alone would produce, so uninsulated apparatus gives a value of c that is too high.

concepts.term: Accurate measurement in this practical (AT 1 and AT 5)
concepts.def: The apparatus and technique skills this practical draws on: recording mass, temperature and time accurately (AT 1), and safely using apparatus such as an immersion heater and joulemeter to measure an energy transfer (AT 5).

concepts.term: Handling the equation and its units (WS and MS)
concepts.def: The mathematical and working-scientifically demands that arise here: converting grams to kilograms, making c the subject of ∆E = m c ∆θ, and evaluating how energy transferred to the surroundings affects the result.

mcqs.q: Which statement gives the specification's definition of the specific heat capacity of a substance?
options: The amount of energy required to raise the temperature of the whole sample by one degree Celsius.
The amount of energy required to raise the temperature of one kilogram of the substance by one degree Celsius.
The thermal energy stored by one kilogram of the substance at a temperature of one degree Celsius.
The rise in temperature produced when one kilogram of the substance is supplied with one joule.
mcqs.explain: The specification's definition: the energy required, for one kilogram of the substance, for a rise of one degree Celsius.

mcqs.q: Which word equation does the specification give for the energy change when a system's temperature changes?
options: change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity × temperature change
change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity ÷ change in temperature
change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity × final temperature
change in thermal energy = specific heat capacity × temperature change
mcqs.explain: The specification's wording exactly: all three quantities are multiplied together.

mcqs.q: A beaker holds 300 g of water at 80 °C. The water is heated until it reaches 100 °C. The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J/kg °C. What is the change in thermal energy of the water?
mcqs.explain: 0.300 kg × 4200 J/kg °C × 20 °C = 25 200 J, with the mass converted to kilograms and ∆θ found by subtraction.

mcqs.q: Water is heated from 18 °C to 78 °C. Which value should be used for ∆θ in ∆E = m c ∆θ, and why?
options: 78 °C, because ∆θ is the temperature that the water reaches.
351 K, because temperatures must be converted into kelvin first.
60 °C, because ∆θ means the change in the temperature.
18 °C, because ∆θ is the temperature the water starts at.
mcqs.explain: ∆ means 'change in', so ∆θ = 78 − 18 = 60 °C, in degrees Celsius as the specification states.

mcqs.q: A 250 g metal block is heated by an immersion heater. The joulemeter shows that 10 000 J has been transferred and the block's temperature rises by 20 °C. What is the specific heat capacity of the metal, in J/kg °C?
mcqs.explain: c = ∆E ÷ (m × ∆θ) = 10 000 ÷ (0.25 × 20) = 2000 J/kg °C, with the mass converted to kilograms.

mcqs.q: Which line gives the units the specification uses for the quantities in ∆E = m c ∆θ?
options: ∆E in J, m in kg, c in J/kg °C, ∆θ in °C
∆E in J, m in kg, c in J/kg °C, ∆θ in kelvin
∆E in J, m in kg, c in J per °C, ∆θ in °C
∆E in J, m in g, c in J/g °C, ∆θ in °C
mcqs.explain: Exactly the units the specification lists: joules, kilograms, joules per kilogram per degree Celsius, and degrees Celsius.

mcqs.q: A hot metal block of mass m cools from 90 °C to 30 °C in still air. What does ∆E = m c ∆θ tell you about the block?
options: Nothing at all, because the equation applies only while a system is being heated up.
Its temperature has fallen, but the energy stored in the block has not changed at all.
The block's thermal energy store has fallen by m × c × 60, and that energy is released.
The block is now storing a total thermal energy of exactly m × c × 30 joules.
mcqs.explain: The specification's equation covers energy released as well as stored, and here ∆θ is 90 − 30 = 60 °C.

mcqs.q: Water has a specific heat capacity of 4200 J/kg °C and aluminium has 900 J/kg °C. What does this tell you?
options: Water heats up faster than aluminium does when both are supplied with the same energy.
Warming 1 kg of water by 1 °C needs more energy than warming 1 kg of aluminium.
A kilogram of water always contains more thermal energy than a kilogram of aluminium.
The temperature rise of a substance is not related to the energy supplied to it.
mcqs.explain: The definition applied directly: 4200 J per kilogram per degree Celsius against 900 J for the aluminium.

mcqs.q: In Required practical activity 1, how is the specific heat capacity of the metal block calculated?
options: By dividing the energy supplied by the mass and by the temperature rise.
By dividing the energy supplied by the temperature rise of the block only.
By dividing the energy supplied by the mass and by the starting temperature of the block.
By multiplying the energy supplied by the mass and by the temperature rise.
mcqs.explain: c = ∆E ÷ (m × ∆θ), which links the decrease of one energy store to the rise in temperature of the block.

mcqs.q: A student heats a metal block with an immersion heater but does not insulate it. The energy supplied is measured accurately with a joulemeter. What is the effect on the calculated value of the specific heat capacity?
options: There is no effect, because all the energy from the heater goes into the block.
It is too low, because the block has gained less energy than the heater supplied.
It is too low, because energy escaping to the room is lost from the total.
It is too high, because some energy warms the room and the temperature rise is smaller.
mcqs.explain: ∆θ is on the bottom of c = ∆E ÷ (m × ∆θ), so a reduced temperature rise makes the calculated c too large.

mcqs.q: Which set of measurements is needed to determine the specific heat capacity of the block in this practical?
options: The mass of the block, the energy supplied by the heater, and the final temperature.
The mass of the block, the energy supplied by the heater, and the temperature rise.
The mass of the block, the power of the heater, and the temperature rise.
The energy supplied by the heater and the temperature rise of the block.
mcqs.explain: These three quantities are exactly what c = ∆E ÷ (m × ∆θ) needs, measured using AT 1 and AT 5 skills.

mcqs.q: Two identical 1 kg blocks of the same metal are heated. Block X rises by 10 °C and block Y rises by 30 °C. Which statement is correct?
options: Block Y has three times the specific heat capacity of X, because it became three times hotter.
Both blocks needed the same energy, because they have the same mass and are the same metal.
Block Y needed three times as much energy as X, because ∆E is proportional to ∆θ.
Block Y now stores three times as much thermal energy in total as block X does.
mcqs.explain: With m and c the same for both, ∆E = m c ∆θ makes the energy transferred proportional to the temperature change.
